P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Partly established. Malawi has exchange controls (Exchange Control Regulation 2022 on repatriation of export proceeds and foreign-currency-denominated accounts). In March 2025 the Reserve Bank cut the mandatory conversion of export proceeds from 30% to 25% for exporters; for NGOs it went from 70% to 50%. Whether and how this applies to individual service exporters (freelancers) was not confirmed.
P1_fx_receipts.note: Press only (Nation Online); regulation text and any rule for individual service exporters not found on 2026-10-22; allAfrica (403).

sources.title: RBM motivates exporters, reviews forex controls (Mar 2025)
sources.quote: Mafuta Mwale: The measures will incentivise the export sector| Among others, he said the central bank has reduced the mandatory conversion ratio on export proceeds from 30 percent to 25 percent for exporters with exemption from the mandatory conversion of export proceeds for manufacturers meeting criteria issued by the central bank.

P1_fx_receipts.notes: Rules described as temporary and under review.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Foreign-currency-denominated accounts (FCDAs) exist and are regulated by the 2022 Exchange Control Regulation. Exporters keep their retained share there. Rules for individuals opening FCDAs were not sourced.
P2_fcy_account.note: No source on individual FCDA eligibility captured on 2026-10-22.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: A sole proprietorship is registered under the Business Registration Act through the online Malawi Business Registration System (MBRS). The registry function reportedly moved from the Registrar General to CRIPC from 1 April 2026. There is no minimum capital and liability is unlimited. Fees were not confirmed (guides cite MK 2,000 to MK 10,000).
L1_registration.note: Single secondary domain (Deel) captured; MBRS/CRIPC official pages not captured on 2026-10-22.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Malawi taxes on a source basis: individuals are taxable on Malawi-source income wherever payment is made. Whether income from services performed in Malawi for foreign clients is Malawi-source (likely, if the work is done in Malawi) was not confirmed. Personal rates reportedly reach 35%.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: Standard VAT 17.5%. The registration threshold doubled from MWK 25m to MWK 50m a year with the 2026–27 budget law, in force 15 April 2026. Foreign digital-service suppliers must now register regardless of turnover. Treatment of exported services was not established.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The Data Protection Act 2024 applies, with MACRA as the authority. Registration is required only for controllers or processors 'of significant importance': those processing personal data of more than 10,000 Malawi residents, or data of significance to the economy, society or security (s. 41(1)). Registration fees were under consultation in July 2026. Cross-border transfers are restricted (s. 38).

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Under the Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act 2016 (s. 35), consumers may withdraw from an electronic contract without reasons or penalty within seven days: of receiving goods, or of forming a services contract (or an agreed period). Suppliers must reimburse within fourteen days, and the consumer may bear return costs. The right does not apply once services have started with the consumer's consent, or to personalised or perishable goods.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving); Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (4) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
